claim: Rats are highly social animals that display complex behaviors including aggression, dominance, mating, parental care, and play.
source: Rats are highly social animals that display complex behaviors (aggression, dominance, mating, parental care, and play [Barnett, 1958]), which involve the use of multi-modal signaling and sensing (Brecht and Freiwald, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barnett, 1958

claim: Social interactions in rats involve the use of multi-modal signaling and sensing.
source: Rats are highly social animals that display complex behaviors (aggression, dominance, mating, parental care, and play [Barnett, 1958]), which involve the use of multi-modal signaling and sensing (Brecht and Freiwald, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brecht and Freiwald, 2012

claim: Social interactions in rats are initially characterized by anogenital sniffing followed by facial contacts which occur at a constant rate.
source: These social interactions are initially characterized by anogenital sniffing followed by facial contacts which occur at a constant rate (Wolfe et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wolfe et al., 2011

claim: Facial contacts have been shown to be involved in dominance-related behaviors in naturalistic settings.
source: Facial contacts have also been shown to be involved in dominance-related behaviors in naturalistic settings (Blanchard et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blanchard et al., 2001

claim: Facial contacts consist of extensive whisker-to-whisker and snout-to-snout touch episodes, largely mediated by macrovibrissae.
source: Facial contacts consist of extensive whisker-to-whisker and snout-to-snout touch episodes, largely mediated by macrovibrissae (Wolfe et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wolfe et al., 2011

claim: The use of macrovibrissae results in a strong activation of the barrel cortex.
source: The use of macrovibrissae results in a strong activation of the barrel cortex and, importantly, the neurons appear to represent the social context of these interactions by distinct firing rates (Bobrov et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bobrov et al., 2014

claim: Barrel cortex neurons appear to represent the social context of interactions by distinct firing rates.
source: The use of macrovibrissae results in a strong activation of the barrel cortex and, importantly, the neurons appear to represent the social context of these interactions by distinct firing rates (Bobrov et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bobrov et al., 2014

claim: Ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) form an important component of rodent social interactions.
source: Ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) form another important component of rodent social interactions (Brudzynski and Pniak, 2002; Wright et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brudzynski and Pniak, 2002 and Wright et al., 2010

claim: Rats produce two distinct classes of USVs: 22 kHz alarm calls and 50 kHz appetitive vocalizations.
source: Rats produce two distinct classes of USVs, 22 kHz alarm calls and 50 kHz appetitive vocalizations (McGinnis and Vakulenko, 2003; Brudzynski, 2009), which serve as indicators of negative and positive affective states, respectively (Knutson et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to McGinnis and Vakulenko, 2003 and Brudzynski, 2009

claim: 22 kHz alarm calls and 50 kHz appetitive vocalizations serve as indicators of negative and positive affective states, respectively.
source: Rats produce two distinct classes of USVs, 22 kHz alarm calls and 50 kHz appetitive vocalizations (McGinnis and Vakulenko, 2003; Brudzynski, 2009), which serve as indicators of negative and positive affective states, respectively (Knutson et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knutson et al., 2002

claim: Alarm calls are elicited by a range of threats including dominant or aggressive conspecifics, predators, and aversive stimuli.
source: While the alarm calls are elicited by a range of threats (dominant or aggressive conspecifics, predators, and aversive stimuli [Brudzynski, 2009]), the 50-kHz calls are produced in anticipation of/in response to direct social contact (Blanchard et al., 1993; Bialy et al., 2000; Brudzynski and Pniak, 2002), mating (Bialy et al., 2000), and homo-specific (rough-and-tumble) or hetero-specific (tickling) play behaviors (Burgdorf et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brudzynski, 2009

claim: 50-kHz calls are produced in anticipation of or in response to direct social contact.
source: While the alarm calls are elicited by a range of threats (dominant or aggressive conspecifics, predators, and aversive stimuli [Brudzynski, 2009]), the 50-kHz calls are produced in anticipation of/in response to direct social contact (Blanchard et al., 1993; Bialy et al., 2000; Brudzynski and Pniak, 2002), mating (Bialy et al., 2000), and homo-specific (rough-and-tumble) or hetero-specific (tickling) play behaviors (Burgdorf et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blanchard et al., 1993; Bialy et al., 2000; Brudzynski and Pniak, 2002

claim: 50-kHz calls are produced during mating.
source: While the alarm calls are elicited by a range of threats (dominant or aggressive conspecifics, predators, and aversive stimuli [Brudzynski, 2009]), the 50-kHz calls are produced in anticipation of/in response to direct social contact (Blanchard et al., 1993; Bialy et al., 2000; Brudzynski and Pniak, 2002), mating (Bialy et al., 2000), and homo-specific (rough-and-tumble) or hetero-specific (tickling) play behaviors (Burgdorf et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bialy et al., 2000

claim: 50-kHz calls are produced during homo-specific (rough-and-tumble) or hetero-specific (tickling) play behaviors.
source: While the alarm calls are elicited by a range of threats (dominant or aggressive conspecifics, predators, and aversive stimuli [Brudzynski, 2009]), the 50-kHz calls are produced in anticipation of/in response to direct social contact (Blanchard et al., 1993; Bialy et al., 2000; Brudzynski and Pniak, 2002), mating (Bialy et al., 2000), and homo-specific (rough-and-tumble) or hetero-specific (tickling) play behaviors (Burgdorf et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burgdorf et al., 2008

claim: Playback experiments have demonstrated that 50-kHz vocalizations can induce approach behavior.
source: Further, playback experiments have demonstrated that 50-kHz vocalizations can induce approach behavior (Wöhr and Schwarting, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wöhr and Schwarting, 2007

claim: Playback of USVs can induce c-fos expression.
source: Studies on the neuronal representation of USVs have largely relied on playback experiments, for example, to demonstrate the induction of c-fos expression (Sadananda et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sadananda et al., 2008

claim: Reliable and preferential responses to USVs have been reported upon playback in anaesthetized rats.
source: Reliable and preferential responses to USVs have been reported upon playback in anaesthetized (Kim and Bao, 2013) or awake rats (Carruthers et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim and Bao, 2013

claim: Reliable and preferential responses to USVs have been reported upon playback in awake rats.
source: Reliable and preferential responses to USVs have been reported upon playback in anaesthetized (Kim and Bao, 2013) or awake rats (Carruthers et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carruthers et al., 2013

claim: A sparse representation of playback sounds has been demonstrated in the awake auditory cortex.
source: However in the awake auditory cortex, a sparse representation of playback sounds has been demonstrated (Hromádka et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hromádka et al., 2008

claim: Experience-dependent modulation of auditory responses by natural odors has been demonstrated in mice.
source: Likewise, there is little information about the integration of multisensory social signals in the auditory cortex, with the notable exception of experience-dependent modulation of auditory responses by natural odors in mice (Cohen et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2011

claim: Rats engaged in extensive facial touch that involved whisker-to-whisker and snout-to-snout contacts with social and non-social stimuli.
source: Rats engaged in extensive facial touch that involved whisker-to-whisker (n = 2894, Figure 1B, left) and snout-to-snout contacts (n = 2232, Figure 1B, right) with social and non-social stimuli (i.e., conspecifics and objects/plastinated rats, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with specific counts and reference to Figure 1B

claim: The interactions were spontaneous, frequent (1.76 events/min), and usually sustained (2.86 ± 2.68 s, mean ± SD).
source: The interactions were spontaneous, frequent (1.76 events/min), and usually sustained (2.86 ± 2.68 s, mean ± SD; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements with specific values

claim: A total of 56,525 USVs were identified and classified into categories described earlier for rats in a social context.
source: A total of 56,525 USVs were identified and classified into categories described earlier for rats in a social context (Wright et al., 2010), that is, trill, complex, flat (Figure 1C), upward ramp, downward ramp, inverted u, split, and short (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with specific count and citation to Wright et al., 2010

claim: 80% of USVs were assigned to a source using intensity measurements from four microphones.
source: Intensity measurements from the four microphones were used to assign a source to the majority of USVs (80%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with specific percentage

claim: More than 4 out of 5 calls were correctly assigned to the source.
source: Analysis of false positive rates estimated that >4 out of 5 calls were correctly assigned to the source (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Supported by analysis of false positive rates described in methods

claim: USVs emitted in three scenarios were predominantly trill, complex, and flat calls.
source: USVs emitted in three scenarios, by the 'Subject alone', by all interacting partners after introduction of stimulus rats ('Social setting'), and during 'Facial touch' were predominantly trill, complex, and flat calls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The proportion of trills increased in social contexts while flats showed a reverse trend.
source: The proportion of trills (red) increased in the social contexts while flats (green) showed a reverse trend.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: All call types were vocalized at a higher rate during facial touch compared to outside of it.
source: All call types were vocalized at a higher rate during facial touch compared to outside of it (even though stimuli were present).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: The baseline calling rate was low when the subject rat was alone (0.13 Hz).
source: While the baseline calling rate was low when the subject rat was alone (0.13 Hz), a substantial increase (0.80 Hz) occurred in the social setting.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements with specific values

claim: A substantial increase in calling rate (0.80 Hz) occurred in the social setting.
source: While the baseline calling rate was low when the subject rat was alone (0.13 Hz), a substantial increase (0.80 Hz) occurred in the social setting.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements with specific values

claim: Within the facial touch episodes, a further increase in vocalization (1.50 Hz) was observed.
source: Within the facial touch episodes, a further increase in vocalization (1.50 Hz) was observed.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements with specific value

claim: The calling rate for all call categories increased during facial touch compared to periods outside of it.
source: Indeed, the calling rate for all call categories increased during facial touch compared to periods outside of it (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), with trills showing the highest increase.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Analysis of peri-stimulus time histograms revealed an increase in calling associated with the onset of facial touch.
source: Analysis of peri-stimulus time histograms (PSTHs) also revealed an increase in calling associated with the onset (Figure 1G) and a sharp decrease with the offset (Figure 1H) of facial touch.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G

claim: A sharp decrease in calling was associated with the offset of facial touch.
source: Analysis of peri-stimulus time histograms (PSTHs) also revealed an increase in calling associated with the onset (Figure 1G) and a sharp decrease with the offset (Figure 1H) of facial touch.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H

claim: For interactions with non-social stimuli, the calling rate was lower (0.36 Hz) and there was no increase in calling during touch.
source: For interactions with non-social stimuli, the calling rate was lower (0.36 Hz) and there was no increase in calling during touch (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I

claim: Calls were typically emitted in the retraction phase of the whisking cycle of the call emitter.
source: As shown in the representative example (Figure 2A), calls were typically emitted in the retraction phase of the whisking cycle of the call emitter (top trace), whereas there was no systematic relationship of calling to the whisking of the interacting partner (bottom trace).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: There was no systematic relationship of calling to the whisking of the interacting partner.
source: As shown in the representative example (Figure 2A), calls were typically emitted in the retraction phase of the whisking cycle of the call emitter (top trace), whereas there was no systematic relationship of calling to the whisking of the interacting partner (bottom trace).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The relationship of call onsets to whisking phase was distributed significantly non-uniformly relative to whisking for call emitter (n = 664, p = 0.0014).
source: We observed that the relationship of call onsets to whisking phase was distributed significantly non-uniformly relative to whisking for call emitter (n = 664, p = 0.0014, Figure 2C, top, Hodges–Anje test) but not for interacting partner (n = 705, p = 0.06, Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: Supported by statistical test (Hodges-Anje test) with specific p-value

claim: The relationship of call onsets to whisking phase was not significantly non-uniform for the interacting partner (n = 705, p = 0.06).
source: We observed that the relationship of call onsets to whisking phase was distributed significantly non-uniformly relative to whisking for call emitter (n = 664, p = 0.0014, Figure 2C, top, Hodges–Anje test) but not for interacting partner (n = 705, p = 0.06, Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: Supported by statistical test (Hodges-Anje test) with specific p-value

claim: There is a substantial bias for calls during the retraction phase of the emitter's whisking (381 in retraction vs 283 in protraction).
source: There also appears to be a substantial bias for calls during the retraction phase of the emitter's whisking (381 in retraction vs 283 in protraction, Figure 2C, top) unlike for calls during the interacting partner's whisking (352 in retraction vs 353 in protraction, Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with specific counts

claim: There is no bias for calls during the retraction phase of the interacting partner's whisking (352 in retraction vs 353 in protraction).
source: There also appears to be a substantial bias for calls during the retraction phase of the emitter's whisking (381 in retraction vs 283 in protraction, Figure 2C, top) unlike for calls during the interacting partner's whisking (352 in retraction vs 353 in protraction, Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with specific counts

claim: The predominant whisking rate during social touch is 8.1 Hz.
source: Predominant whisking rates determined by power spectral density of whisker traces during social touch is 8.1 Hz (left).
evidence: Supported by power spectral density analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: The distribution of time intervals between whisking cycles within one animal shows a peak at ca. 112 ms.
source: Distribution of time intervals between whisking cycles within one animal (auto) correspondingly shows a peak at ca. 112 ms (middle).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The predominant calling rate is 7.6 Hz.
source: Power spectral density analysis to determine the predominant calling rates revealed a 7.6 Hz predominant frequency component (left).
evidence: Supported by power spectral density analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: Interacting animals do not whisk with a fixed phase relationship.
source: Inter-animal (cross) whisking interval distribution suggests that the interacting animals do not whisk with a fixed phase relationship (right).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Whisking is not coordinated across animals.
source: This was consistent with previous observations that whisking is not coordinated across animals (Wolfe et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wolfe et al., 2011

claim: The coordination of whisking and vocalization is restricted to individuals.
source: Such rhythmicity was not obvious when the call onsets across interaction partners were analyzed ('cross', Figure 2E, right), suggesting that the coordination of whisking and vocalization is restricted to individuals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and inference from the data

claim: Most auditory cortex neurons showed little or no response to calls.
source: Strikingly, most auditory cortex neurons showed little or no response to calls while ∼10% of RS neurons showed heterogeneous and excitatory responses (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Approximately 10% of RS neurons showed heterogeneous and excitatory responses to calls.
source: Strikingly, most auditory cortex neurons showed little or no response to calls while ∼10% of RS neurons showed heterogeneous and excitatory responses (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Some RS neurons had a fast onset-associated response (response latency <25 ms of call onset).
source: Some RS neurons had a fast onset-associated response (response latency <25 ms of call onset; Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B), while the others showed a more sustained response (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Some RS neurons showed a more sustained response to calls.
source: Some RS neurons had a fast onset-associated response (response latency <25 ms of call onset; Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B), while the others showed a more sustained response (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: A few late responders were observed (response latency >50 ms after call onset).
source: In addition, a few late responders were also observed (response latency >50 ms after call onset; Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure

claim: USVs elicited a small (∼5%) but significant increase in the population of RS neurons sampled.
source: USVs elicited a small (∼5%) but significant increase in the population of RS neurons sampled (Figure 3B, left), as reflected in their firing rates (mean response to all calls ± SEM: 9.3 ± 0.82 Hz vs baseline: 8.8 ± 0.77 Hz; n = 172, p = 0.0006, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific p-value and experimental data

claim: The mean firing rate of RS neurons in response to all calls was 9.3 ± 0.82 Hz vs baseline of 8.8 ± 0.77 Hz (n = 172, p = 0.0006).
source: USVs elicited a small (∼5%) but significant increase in the population of RS neurons sampled (Figure 3B, left), as reflected in their firing rates (mean response to all calls ± SEM: 9.3 ± 0.82 Hz vs baseline: 8.8 ± 0.77 Hz; n = 172, p = 0.0006, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific values and p-value

claim: The median firing rates of RS neurons were lower (response to calls: 6.06 Hz vs baseline: 5.42 Hz).
source: The median firing rates however were lower (response to calls: 6.06 Hz vs baseline: 5.42 Hz).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements with specific values

claim: The overall increase in the mean firing rate was contributed to by a small fraction of neurons within the population.
source: This would suggest that the overall increase in the mean firing rate was contributed to by a small fraction of neurons within the population.
evidence: Inferred from the difference between mean and median firing rates

claim: FS neurons showed a robust excitatory modulation by USVs.
source: FS neurons on the other hand showed a robust excitatory modulation by USVs (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Most FS neurons had a sustained response to calls.
source: Most FS neurons had a sustained response to calls (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Few FS cells with sharp short latency or delayed responses were observed.
source: In addition, few cells with sharp short latency (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G) or delayed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H) responses were also observed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The mean firing rates of FS neurons showed a consistent upregulation (response to calls: 19.11 ± 3.94 Hz vs baseline: 16.92 ± 4.07 Hz, n = 23, p = 0.006).
source: The mean firing rates showed a consistent upregulation (response to calls: 19.11 ± 3.94 Hz vs baseline: 16.92 ± 4.07 Hz, n = 23, p = 0.006, Wilcoxon signed rank test), which is seen in the scatter plots (Figure 3D, left).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific values and p-value

claim: Many neurons (RS and FS) responded to more than one of the major call categories.
source: Analysis of call category specificity revealed that many neurons (RS and FS) responded to more than one of the major call categories (Figure 3A,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C,D,F–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: There is a significant modulation of RS neurons by all the major call categories.
source: Population level analysis showed that there is a significant modulation of RS neurons by all the major call categories (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, top row).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure

claim: FS neurons appear to be significantly modulated by trills alone.
source: FS neurons however appear to be significantly modulated by trills alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure

claim: There appears to be no overwhelming population of trill-/complex-/flat-preferring neurons.
source: While this scenario biased towards larger effects shows a highly significant modulation by the 'best call' (p < 0.0001, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), there appears to be no overwhelming population of trill-/complex-/flat-preferring neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure

claim: RS neurons significantly responded to calls from the stimulus animals but not to the subject animal's own calls.
source: We also determined that while RS neurons significantly responded to calls from the stimulus animals, this was not the case with the subject animal's own calls (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, top row).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure

claim: A pair-wise comparison of each RS neuron's response to own vs stimulus calls was not significantly different (p = 0.85).
source: However, a pair-wise comparison of each RS neuron's response to own vs stimulus calls was not significantly different (p = 0.85, Wilcoxon signed rank test), suggesting that this was a population level effect.
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific p-value

claim: FS neurons showed a clear preference for own calls but not for the stimulus calls.
source: Interestingly, the reverse was true for the FS neurons, which showed a clear preference for own calls but not for the stimulus calls (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure

claim: Pairwise comparisons of FS neuronal responses showed a significant difference (p = 0.03) between own and stimulus calls.
source: Pairwise comparisons of FS neuronal responses showed a significant difference (p = 0.03), suggesting that they could indeed discriminate between own and stimulus calls.
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific p-value

claim: FS neurons could discriminate between own and stimulus calls.
source: Pairwise comparisons of FS neuronal responses showed a significant difference (p = 0.03), suggesting that they could indeed discriminate between own and stimulus calls.
evidence: Inferred from the significant difference in pairwise comparisons

claim: AuD and Au1 RS neurons were significantly modulated by USVs.
source: AuD and Au1 RS neurons as well as Au1 FS neurons were significantly modulated by USVs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B

claim: Au1 FS neurons were significantly modulated by USVs.
source: AuD and Au1 RS neurons as well as Au1 FS neurons were significantly modulated by USVs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B

claim: At the population level, there was no strong preference to the whisking phase.
source: At the population level, there was no strong preference to the whisking phase (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure

claim: Facial touch resulted in an inhibition of several RS and FS neurons.
source: Unexpectedly, we observed that facial touch resulted in an inhibition of several RS (Figure 4A–D) and FS (Figure 4E–G) neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: A substantial fraction of neurons in the dataset showed a distinct off-response (∼19%).
source: A substantial fraction of neurons in our dataset showed this distinct off-response (∼19%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with specific percentage

claim: The off-response phenomenon appears to occur in Au1 but not in the other auditory cortex sub-regions.
source: This phenomenon appears to occur in Au1 (Figure 4C) but not in the other auditory cortex sub-regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: In Au1 RS neurons, the firing rates reduced from 8.18 ± 1.03 Hz to 7.82 ± 1.04 Hz during the touch episode (n = 105, p = 0.0067).
source: In Au1 RS neurons, the firing rates reduced from 8.18 ± 1.03 Hz to 7.82 ± 1.04 Hz during the touch episode (n = 105, p = 0.0067, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 4C, left).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific values and p-value

claim: Compared to touch, the firing rate in the off-response window was significantly higher at 8.49 ± 1.1 Hz (n = 105, p = 0.0019).
source: Compared to touch, the firing rate in the off-response window was significantly higher at 8.49 ± 1.1 Hz (n = 105, p = 0.0019, Figure 4C, right).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific values and p-value

claim: The ∼10% increase in the population response was about twice as large as the excitatory responses elicited by USVs in RS cells.
source: Unexpectedly, this ∼10% increase in the population response was about twice as large as the excitatory responses elicited by USVs in RS cells.
evidence: Comparison of experimental data from different conditions

claim: For Au1 FS neurons, the baseline firing rates decreased from 14.6 ± 4.18 Hz to 13.82 ± 4.03 Hz due to touch (n = 15, p = 0.0302).
source: Similarly, for Au1 FS neurons, the baseline firing rates decreased from 14.6 ± 4.18 Hz to 13.82 ± 4.03 Hz due to touch (n = 15, p = 0.0302, Figure 4F, left).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific values and p-value

claim: The firing rate during the off-response window was higher at 17.03 ± 4.71 Hz when compared to the touch episode (p = 0.0043).
source: The firing rate during the off-response window was higher at 17.03 ± 4.71 Hz when compared to the touch episode (p = 0.0043, Figure 4F, right).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific values and p-value

claim: The off-response to facial touch was the largest population response observed in the auditory cortex.
source: The off-response to facial touch is remarkable as it was the largest population response we observed in the auditory cortex.
evidence: Comparison of experimental data across different conditions

claim: Mean response indices for Au1 RS neurons showed that the overall inhibition due to touch was reversed after the touch episode (p = 0.0329).
source: Mean response indices for Au1 RS neurons (Figure 4D) showed that the overall inhibition due to touch was reversed after the touch episode (p = 0.0329).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific p-value

claim: A similar inhibition at touch onset and reversal at the end of touch were evident in Au1 FS neurons (p = 0.0026).
source: A similar inhibition at touch onset and reversal at the end of touch were also evident in Au1 FS neurons (p = 0.0026, Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific p-value

claim: Sound intensity measurements did not show any increase in intensity due to whisker movement and contacts.
source: Sound intensity measurements were performed but no change was detected due to whisker movement and contacts, at least at the microphones.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: USVs lead to a large increase in sound intensity as expected.
source: USVs lead to a large increase as expected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure

claim: In RS neurons, the response to calls was modulated by touch.
source: Indeed, we observed that in RS neurons, the response to calls was modulated by touch (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure

claim: Pairwise comparison of each neuron's response to USVs in and out of touch revealed a highly significant differential modulation (p = 0.0038).
source: Pairwise comparison of each neuron's response to USVs in (right) and out (left) of touch revealed a highly significant differential modulation (p = 0.0038, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific p-value

claim: Response indices of RS neurons to calls out of touch were largely centered around zero indicating little or no modulation.
source: While response indices of RS neurons to calls out of touch were largely centered around zero indicating little or no modulation (Figure 5C, left), they were more spread out during touch (Figure 5C, right) indicating significantly greater modulation (p = 0.0072, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure

claim: Response indices of RS neurons were more spread out during touch indicating significantly greater modulation (p = 0.0072).
source: While response indices of RS neurons to calls out of touch were largely centered around zero indicating little or no modulation (Figure 5C, left), they were more spread out during touch (Figure 5C, right) indicating significantly greater modulation (p = 0.0072, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific p-value

claim: In FS neurons, responsiveness to calls appeared to be less strongly modulated by touch at the individual and population levels (p = 0.3303).
source: However, in FS neurons, responsiveness to calls appeared to be less strongly modulated by touch at the individual (Figure 5D) and population levels (p = 0.3303, Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific p-value

claim: The spread of activation indices in FS neurons did not differ in and out of touch (p = 0.3752).
source: Correspondingly, the spread of activation indices did not differ in and out of touch (p = 0.3752, Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific p-value

claim: Bootstrapped data show that neuronal responses in RS (but not FS) neurons were strongly modulated during touch, independent of the number of samples.
source: These bootstrapped data show that neuronal responses in RS (but not FS) neurons were strongly modulated during touch, independent of the number of samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by bootstrapping analysis shown in figures

claim: There does not appear to be any greater responsiveness to stimulus calls during touch.
source: There, however, does not appear to be any greater responsiveness to stimulus calls during touch.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: The intensity differences are probably not responsible for the higher modulation during touch.
source: This would suggest that the intensity differences are probably not responsible for the higher modulation during touch (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of greater responsiveness to stimulus calls during touch

claim: The responsiveness to USVs in the auditory cortex is modulated by facial touch.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the responsiveness to USVs in the auditory cortex is modulated by facial touch.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing differential modulation

claim: Social transmission of food preference relies on the combined use of olfactory and gustatory cues.
source: Social transmission of food preference which relies on the combined use of olfactory and gustatory cues (Galef and Wigmore, 1983) is probably the most extensively studied example of this.
evidence: Supported by citation to Galef and Wigmore, 1983

claim: The use of unimodal signals including vision (ear wiggling), smell (cheek gland pheromones), and somatosensation has been reported.
source: In addition, the use of unimodal signals including vision (ear wiggling [Erskine, 1989]), smell (cheek gland pheromones, [Kannan and Archunan, 2001], and somatosensation [Blanchard et al., 2001]) has also been reported.
evidence: Supported by citations to Erskine, 1989; Kannan and Archunan, 2001; Blanchard et al., 2001

claim: Facial touch during social interactions is associated with an increased production of USVs.
source: We demonstrate that facial touch during social interactions is associated with an increased production of USVs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: There is a temporal coordination of vocalization and whisking, with calls being associated with the retraction of whiskers.
source: We observe a temporal coordination of vocalization and whisking, with calls being associated with the retraction of whiskers.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: USVs elicited excitatory responses in a small fraction of RS neurons in the auditory cortex.
source: USVs elicited excitatory responses in a small fraction of RS neurons in the auditory cortex, whereas almost all FS neurons showed a strong activation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: Almost all FS neurons showed a strong activation in response to USVs.
source: USVs elicited excitatory responses in a small fraction of RS neurons in the auditory cortex, whereas almost all FS neurons showed a strong activation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: Facial touch resulted in a robust inhibition of the primary auditory cortex.
source: Facial touch however resulted in a robust inhibition of the primary auditory cortex.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: A remarkable off-response was observed at the end of the touch episode, possibly reflecting a release of touch-induced inhibition.
source: Moreover, we observed a remarkable off-response at the end of the touch episode, possibly reflecting a release of touch-induced inhibition, which was surprisingly the largest response modulation observed in our study.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and speculation about mechanism

claim: The off-response was the largest response modulation observed in the study.
source: Moreover, we observed a remarkable off-response at the end of the touch episode, possibly reflecting a release of touch-induced inhibition, which was surprisingly the largest response modulation observed in our study.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: The response of auditory cortex neurons to USVs is modulated by facial touch.
source: Finally, it appears that the response of auditory cortex neurons to USVs is modulated by facial touch.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: Spontaneously interacting rats use their whiskers for extensive facial interactions.
source: Previous studies from our laboratory have used the gap paradigm to study social interactions and have demonstrated that spontaneously interacting rats use their whiskers for extensive facial interactions (Wolfe et al., 2011; von Heimendahl et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wolfe et al., 2011 and von Heimendahl et al., 2012

claim: The social context (sex and sexual status) of interactions appears to be represented in the barrel cortex neurons.
source: Interestingly, the social context (sex and sexual status) of these interactions appears to be represented in the barrel cortex neurons (Bobrov et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bobrov et al., 2014

claim: USVs contribute to species-specific social signaling.
source: A little explored component of these interactions has been USVs, which are known to contribute to species-specific social signaling (Brudzynski and Pniak, 2002; Brudzynski, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brudzynski and Pniak, 2002 and Brudzynski, 2013

claim: A reduction in social interaction and ultrasonic communication has been reported in a mouse model of monogenic heritable autism.
source: A reduction in social interaction and ultrasonic communication has also been reported in a mouse model of monogenic heritable autism (Jamain et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jamain et al., 2008

claim: Using the gap paradigm, an increase in the rate of vocalizations was observed during the presentation of social (but not non-social) stimuli.
source: Indeed, using the gap paradigm, we observed an increase in the rate of vocalizations during the presentation of social (but not non-social) stimuli.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: The calling rate showed a sharp decrease at the end of interactions.
source: Interestingly, the calling rate also showed a sharp decrease at the end of interactions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: A vast majority of calls in the paradigm belong to one of the three categories: trill, complex, and flat.
source: We observe that a vast majority of calls in our paradigm belong to one of the three categories that is, trill, complex, and flat.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: The proportion of trills and flats appear to be modulated by the presence of conspecifics.
source: Further, the proportion of trills and flats appear to be modulated by the presence of conspecifics.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: There is a greater prevalence of flats in singly tested rats whereas trill vocalization is increased in pair-tested rats.
source: These results are in line with the finding that there is a greater prevalence of flats in singly tested rats whereas trill vocalization is increased in pair-tested rats (Wright et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wright et al., 2010

claim: A role for trills in social contexts has been reported during play behavior.
source: A role for trills in social contexts has also been reported during play behavior (Schwarting et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwarting et al., 2007

claim: Specific call categories could play a role during specific components of social interactions.
source: Taken together, these results would suggest that specific call categories could play a role during specific components of social interactions.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing modulation of call types by social context

claim: Male mice emit distinct vocalizations when females leave the environment.
source: This idea is supported by a recent study which reports that male mice emit distinct vocalizations when females leave the environment (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2013

claim: A locking of calling to whisking was observed, with calls being produced during the retraction phase of the whisking cycle.
source: We observed a locking of calling to whisking, with calls being produced during the retraction phase of the whisking cycle.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: The retraction phase has been correlated to the exhalation phase of breathing.
source: The retraction phase has been correlated to the exhalation phase of breathing (Moore et al., 2013), which would correspond to call production.
evidence: Supported by citation to Moore et al., 2013

claim: Sniffing and whisking are tightly correlated.
source: Previous studies have shown that in addition to a correlation of respiration and USV production (Roberts, 1972; Riede, 2011), sniffing and whisking are also tightly correlated (Welker, 1964; Ranade et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Welker, 1964 and Ranade et al., 2013

claim: Respiration and USV production are correlated.
source: Previous studies have shown that in addition to a correlation of respiration and USV production (Roberts, 1972; Riede, 2011), sniffing and whisking are also tightly correlated (Welker, 1964; Ranade et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Roberts, 1972 and Riede, 2011

claim: The neural substrate of coordination between whisking and breathing is thought to lie in the joint architecture of pattern generators for whisking and breathing.
source: The neural substrate of such coordination is thought to lie in the joint architecture of pattern generators for whisking and breathing (Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moore et al., 2013

claim: There is a selective increase in the representation of sounds repeated at an ethological rate.
source: Further, our results on the ∼8 Hz vocalization rate are in line with an earlier report that there is a selective increase in the representation of sounds repeated at an ethological rate (Kim and Bao, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim and Bao, 2009

claim: RS neurons in the auditory cortex largely had little or no response to USVs.
source: RS neurons in the auditory cortex largely had little or no response to USVs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: A very small fraction (∼10%) of RS neurons showed robust responses to calls.
source: A very small fraction (∼10%) however showed robust responses to calls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: This is the first report of neuronal responses to conspecific calls in awake behaving rats.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report of neuronal responses to conspecific calls in awake behaving rats.
evidence: Based on knowledge of the literature

claim: Previous reports on the neuronal encoding of USVs in the rat auditory cortex have employed playback experiments in anesthetized preparations or awake rats.
source: Previous reports on the neuronal encoding of USVs in the rat auditory cortex have employed playback experiments in anesthetized preparations (Kim and Bao, 2013) or awake rats (Carruthers et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim and Bao, 2013 and Carruthers et al., 2013

claim: Previous studies report reliable population responses to vocalizations.
source: While these studies report reliable population responses to vocalizations, our data are very similar to another study that shows that there is a sparse representation of sounds in the unanaesthetized auditory cortex (Hromádka et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Less than 5% of neurons responded robustly to sounds at any instant in the unanaesthetized auditory cortex.
source: Using a method that is not biased to neuronal activity (cell-attached recordings), the authors report that <5% of neurons responded robustly to sounds at any instant.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hromádka et al., 2008

claim: Narrow-spiking inter-neurons are highly responsive to sounds.
source: Further, they also report that narrow-spiking inter-neurons are highly responsive.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hromádka et al., 2008

claim: Most cells displayed early (<25 ms after call onset) increases in firing rates.
source: Of the strongly modulated neurons, we observe a range of responses: most cells displayed early (<25 ms after call onset) increases in firing rates, while a few late responders (>50 ms after call onset) were also observed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: Responses tended to be sharp or sustained.
source: Responses tended to be sharp or sustained, with a few cells showing robust modulation by one or more call categories.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: At the population level, the major call categories evoked strong activation in the RS cell population.
source: At the population level, the major call categories evoked strong activation in the RS cell population whereas FS neurons appear to be modulated only by trills.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: There does not appear to be any population level preference for one of the major call types with relation to their best response.
source: Also, there does not appear to be any population level preference for one of these call types with relation to their best response.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: RS neurons seem to prefer the stimulus calls whereas FS neurons were strongly modulated by the animal's own calls.
source: Interestingly, RS neurons seem to prefer the stimulus calls whereas FS neurons were strongly modulated by the animal's own calls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: A cell-wise analysis of response to own vs stimulus calls does not show any difference, suggesting that this phenomenon is brought out at the population level.
source: However, a cell-wise analysis of response to own vs stimulus calls does not show any difference, suggesting that this phenomenon is brought out at the population level.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference

claim: There appears to be auditory cortex sub-region-wise differences, in that AuD and Au1 respond significantly to calls.
source: There also appears to be auditory cortex sub-region-wise differences, in that AuD and Au1 respond significantly to calls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: Despite the temporal coordination of whisking and calling, there is no strong preference of the auditory cortex to the whisking phase at the population level.
source: Despite the temporal coordination of whisking and calling, we do not observe any strong preference of the auditory cortex to the whisking phase at the population level.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: An anatomical basis for multisensory responses in auditory cortex lies in the direct connectivity between somatosensory and auditory cortices.
source: An anatomical basis for these observations would lie in the direct connectivity between somatosensory and auditory cortices (Budinger et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Budinger et al., 2006

claim: Multisensory integration of sound and touch has been shown to occur in the dorsal cochlear nucleus.
source: Even prior to the cortical processing, multisensory integration of sound and touch has been shown to occur in the dorsal cochlear nucleus (Young et al., 1995; Kanold and Young, 2001; Shore, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Young et al., 1995; Kanold and Young, 2001; Shore, 2005

claim: A possible role for touch in the auditory areas is to enhance responses to non-self vocalizations while suppressing responses to self-generated sounds.
source: It has also been suggested that a possible role for touch in the auditory areas is to enhance responses to non-self vocalizations while at the same time suppressing responses to self-generated sounds such as calls or respiration (Shore and Zhou, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shore and Zhou, 2006

claim: Multisensory integration of visual information in the auditory cortex has been demonstrated in ferrets.
source: Multisensory integration of visual (Bizley et al., 2007) and olfactory information (Cohen et al., 2011) in the auditory cortex has been demonstrated in ferrets and rats, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bizley et al., 2007

claim: Multisensory integration of olfactory information in the auditory cortex has been demonstrated in rats.
source: Multisensory integration of visual (Bizley et al., 2007) and olfactory information (Cohen et al., 2011) in the auditory cortex has been demonstrated in ferrets and rats, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2011

claim: Evidence for multisensory integration in the primary auditory cortex comes from studies on the modulation by touch in primates.
source: Evidence for multisensory integration in the primary auditory cortex also comes from studies on the modulation by touch (Fu et al., 2003; Kayser et al., 2005) and vision (Kayser et al., 2007) in primates.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fu et al., 2003 and Kayser et al., 2005

claim: Evidence for multisensory integration in the primary auditory cortex comes from studies on the modulation by vision in primates.
source: Evidence for multisensory integration in the primary auditory cortex also comes from studies on the modulation by touch (Fu et al., 2003; Kayser et al., 2005) and vision (Kayser et al., 2007) in primates.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kayser et al., 2007

claim: It has been reported that balanced inhibition underlies tuning and sharpens spike timing in auditory cortex.
source: It has been reported that balanced inhibition underlies tuning and sharpens spike timing in auditory cortex (Wehr and Zador, 2003) and that inhibition might contribute to auditory processing (Hamilton et al., 2013; Shamma, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wehr and Zador, 2003

claim: Inhibition might contribute to auditory processing.
source: It has been reported that balanced inhibition underlies tuning and sharpens spike timing in auditory cortex (Wehr and Zador, 2003) and that inhibition might contribute to auditory processing (Hamilton et al., 2013; Shamma, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hamilton et al., 2013 and Shamma, 2013
